soil-fert-285.title: Manganese: the chlorophyll helper
soil-fert-285.text: Plants short of manganese turn yellow between the leaf veins, a pattern called chlorosis. Manganese activates some enzymes involved in chlorophyll formation, and it is one of the micronutrients in {{ref:soil-fert-179}}. Its availability depends partly on soil pH. The facts add that plants need only trace amounts of nickel, as with other micronutrients. Some plants use molybdenum for {{ref:soil-fert-100}}, so it may need adding to some soils before legumes are sown.

soil-form-002.title: The soil profile, a record read from the top down
soil-form-002.text: Going down a soil profile means going back in time. Like layers of sediment, its horizons record past events. A soil profile is a vertical face of soil showing its horizons, layers roughly parallel to the surface. Formally, it is one face of the three-dimensional block described in {{ref:soil-form-003}}. Soil scientists expose a profile by digging a pit or extracting a core with a hand or hydraulic push tube or an auger. Mature profiles typically have three basic master horizons, A, B and C, but no profile has all the major horizons. Some soils, such as those of the {{ref:soil-class-094}} order, have only one horizon or none. Young soils on mine waste, moraines, volcanic cones, dunes or alluvial terraces are examples. Wind or running water can strip the upper horizons and bury them downslope, a natural process that {{ref:soil-agri-095}} aggravates. Major earthworks or regular deep plowing can leave a soil almost without distinct horizons. The horizons also hold clues to the past. Pollen, {{ref:soil-bio-195}} and plant remains can reveal changes in climate or how the land was used, and large pieces of charcoal allow dating by the method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}}.

soil-form-062.title: Cheluviation: metals ride organic carriers downward
soil-form-062.text: A gray-white leached layer above a dark brown or red one is a typical signature of cheluviation. In this process, metal ions in the upper soil bind with organic molecules called ligands, forming chelates. The chelates move downward by eluviation and are then deposited. Iron, aluminum, manganese, calcium, magnesium and {{ref:soil-fert-290}} can all be chelated, mostly by ligands from soil organic matter. Chelates with the organic acid described in {{ref:soil-chem-060}} leach and deposit strongly. Iron and aluminum move easily at low pH and under reducing conditions, but precipitate as pH rises to around 7–8 or under oxidizing conditions. Clay adsorbs chelates and weakens their leaching, while coarse-textured or water-saturated soils enhance it.

soil-form-140.title: Primary minerals, inherited unchanged from rock
soil-form-140.text: Much of a soil's grit was never made in the soil at all. Soil minerals come in two types. Primary minerals are found in soil but did not form there. They crystallized with their host igneous rock and have not been chemically altered since. Secondary minerals, by contrast, form as primary minerals weather. Primary mineral particles are mostly larger than 2 μm. They make up the silt, sand and gravel fractions. {{ref:soil-form-135}} supplies them: quartz, {{ref:soil-form-141}}, {{ref:soil-form-142}}, {{ref:soil-chem-226}}, {{ref:soil-form-144}}, amphibole, pyroxene and {{ref:soil-form-145}}. Silicates dominate the primary minerals in soil, and quartz and cristobalite are common soil tectosilicates, silicates built as a three-dimensional framework. The chain runs from primary rocks, the source of primary minerals, to the parent rocks those minerals compose.

soil-form-162.title: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon
soil-form-162.text: No other part of Canada has soils as varied as British Columbia and Yukon, thanks to a varied geologic history, rugged terrain and a wide climate range. The region holds all ten soil orders of the Canadian system. {{ref:soil-class-138}} soils have the largest extent in British Columbia, on {{ref:soil-chem-004}} under cool, humid conditions, and {{ref:soil-class-133}} soils are the other dominant order, on loamy glacial tills in the Interior plateaus and boreal forest. Cryosols occur in areas of permanently frozen ground of northern Yukon and on high mountain peaks, while {{ref:soil-class-123}} soils occur only in the arid Central Interior. {{ref:soil-class-139}} soils mark landslide-prone and avalanche-prone slopes and the Fraser Delta, and drained {{ref:soil-class-127}} soils in the Fraser Valley are among the province's most productive farm soils. Mining leaves {{ref:soil-class-044}}; in metal mining the chief concern is acid rock drainage, because sulphide minerals such as {{ref:soil-chem-134}} weather rapidly to sulfuric acid.

soil-form-166.title: Soils of Ontario
soil-form-166.text: Ontario's soils are young, laid down by the Wisconsinan Laurentide Ice Sheet. The ice retreated northeast, exposing southern Ontario as much as 13,000 years ago and the far north about 8,500 to 6,500 years ago. Three ecozones now dominate. The Hudson Plains (about 25% of Ontario) are cold and semi-arid, with clayey and silty glacio-marine materials over neutral to alkaline limestones. The Boreal Shield (about 66%) lies on acidic, weathering-resistant Precambrian gneiss and granite, and Dystric Brunisols dominate the west. The Mixedwood Plains (about 9%) rest on carbonate-rich limestones, so parent material matters most; they hold the province's most productive farmland and its major cities. The Guelph series, a Brunisolic Gray-Brown {{ref:soil-class-133}} formed in moraine of {{ref:soil-phys-012}} to silty texture, became Ontario's provincial soil in 2015.

soil-form-172.title: Hydrolysis: how water cracks minerals open
soil-form-172.text: Water does more than wet a mineral; it can break it. Hydrolysis is any chemical reaction in which a water molecule breaks one or more chemical bonds. One fragment of the split molecule gains a hydrogen ion and the other gains a hydroxide. It is the reverse of condensation, which joins molecules by removing water. The lab manual says all minerals weather this way, and that hydrolysis is the primary reaction releasing most plant nutrient elements from minerals. In one example, {{ref:soil-form-143}} and water yield an aluminum silicate, K+ and OH-. This is a main route of {{ref:soil-found-058}}. Hydrolysis also drives {{ref:soil-chem-076}}. Metal ions in water form aqua ions that act as acids: trivalent Al3+ and Fe3+ are weak acids with a pKa comparable to acetic acid, while Na+ hydrolyses almost imperceptibly. In the soils of {{ref:soil-chem-030}}, loosely bound Al3+ and Fe3+ and sparingly soluble sulfates such as {{ref:soil-chem-197}} release H+ this way. In the soils of {{ref:soil-chem-019}} the carbonate anion hydrolyses to bicarbonate and hydroxyl ions, raising pH. The enzyme {{ref:soil-fert-224}} catalyzes the hydrolysis of {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, and highly alkaline soils, pH about 8.2 or higher, increase it.

soil-found-001.title: Soil horizons, the layers that record a soil's life
soil-found-001.text: Cut down through a soil and you usually cross a series of bands. Each band is a horizon: a layer roughly parallel to the surface whose physical, chemical and biological traits differ from those above and below. Horizons are made by {{ref:soil-form-155}}. Layers those processes have not touched are simply called layers. Given time, an undifferentiated soil evolves a profile of two or more horizons. They differ greatly in thickness and generally lack sharp boundaries. Most are recognized by color and texture, described outright or relative to their neighbors, as coarser, sandier or darker. No profile has every major horizon, and some soils, such as soils described in {{ref:soil-class-094}}, have one horizon or none at all. Horizons are also fragile. Erosion can strip the upper ones and bury others downslope, and tillage, tree growth and major earthworks disturb or erase them. Going down a profile goes back in time. Pollen, {{ref:soil-bio-195}} and plant remains record past environmental change, and charcoal allows a horizon to be dated by the method in {{ref:soil-hist-120}}. Most classification systems define soil types by horizons, either as whole sequences, as in the German system, or as selected diagnostic horizons. A shorthand of letters and numbers labels each one, recording color, texture, structure, consistency, roots, pH, voids, boundaries and nodules.

soil-found-025.title: Soil color, the first thing anyone notices
soil-found-025.text: Soils come brown, red, yellow, black, gray, white and even blue or green. Color is often a soil's most visually apparent property and the first impression it makes. It varies across landscapes, between horizons and even within a single clod. Color itself does not change how a soil behaves. It forms through chemical and biological weathering, especially the reactions described in {{ref:soil-chem-113}}. Elements released from the original minerals combine into new colored compounds. Ordinary conditions give uniform or gradual changes in color. Reducing environments, short of oxygen, produce disrupted, mottled patterns with points of concentrated color. Mineralogy is the main influence. Because color, especially its lightness, changes with moisture, it may be described both moist and dry. Sources disagree on what color is worth. One says it has little use in predicting soil characteristics. Another says it reveals {{ref:soil-found-045}}, mineralogy, moisture and how much has been washed out.

soil-found-038.title: Scratch, streak and shine: telling minerals apart
soil-found-038.text: Color is the most obvious thing about a mineral, and often not diagnostic at all. Mineral identification tells minerals apart by physical properties: crystal habit, hardness, luster, color, streak, cleavage and specific gravity. Hardness is usually measured on the Mohs scale of scratch resistance, which runs through ten indicator minerals from talc to diamond. The streak is the color of the powdered mineral, and traces of other elements and weathering do not change it. Some minerals can only be classified by optical, chemical or {{ref:soil-chem-228}} analysis, which can be costly and time-consuming. Even grains too small to see have a periodic crystal structure that it can determine.

soil-found-041.title: How rain and time turn feldspar into clay
soil-found-041.text: Granite carries the makings of clay. One of its minerals, a kind of {{ref:soil-form-141}} described in {{ref:soil-form-143}}, weathers to {{ref:soil-chem-088}} and silicic acid, releasing potassium ions. Clay formation is the making of {{ref:soil-chem-079}}, most commonly by long chemical weathering of silicate-bearing rocks, and their gathering into deposits. The work is done largely by acid {{ref:soil-form-172}}. Weak carbonic acid in rainwater, or acid released by plant roots, breaks the bonds between aluminum and oxygen. Other metal ions and silica come loose, the silica as a gel of orthosilicic acid. Source rock and climate decide the product. Feldspar-rich rock gives kaolin under warm, acid weathering, and {{ref:soil-chem-094}} under alkaline conditions. Under alkaline conditions, the rock of {{ref:soil-form-135}} yields {{ref:soil-chem-091}}. Intense weathering of other such minerals produces an aluminum hydroxide. Hydrothermal activity can also make them locally. Then the clay may travel. Primary clays stay where they formed, as residual soil deposits. Secondary clays are carried off by flowing water and laid down elsewhere, often in large lakes or marine basins.

soil-found-045.title: Soil organic matter: the small fraction that shapes everything
soil-found-045.text: Soil organic matter is present in small amounts, typically 1 to 6% by weight in agricultural soil, yet it strongly affects almost all soil properties. It is about twice the organic carbon level. Its parts are described as the living, the dead and the very dead. They are living organisms, fresh residues, and molecules from well-decomposed residues. The living part is about 15% of soil organic matter, and soil organisms are estimated at about 25% of the world's biodiversity. Fresh residues, the active fraction, feed soil organisms and release nutrients. Easily decomposed molecules like proteins, amino acids, sugars and starches do not last long, while {{ref:soil-bio-116}} decomposes more slowly. Waterlogged peats and mucks hold much undecomposed organic matter that does not give the benefits of fresh residues. Organic matter also builds structure. Sticky substances on earthworm skin and fungal products bind particles, and sticky root substances plus fine roots and mycorrhizae promote stable aggregates. Organic compounds produced as fresh residues decompose also bind soil particles and give good structure. Earthworms and some fungi make channels that improve infiltration, water status and aeration. The link to {{ref:soil-bio-001}} is direct, since the living part is the soil's biology.

soil-phys-004.title: Aggregate stability: will the crumbs hold together?
soil-phys-004.text: A soil can look healthy and still fall apart in the first hard rain. Soil aggregate stability measures how well aggregates resist breaking apart under forces such as water and wind erosion, shrinking and swelling, and tillage. It describes {{ref:soil-phys-001}}, responds to management and serves as a soil-quality indicator because it combines physical, chemical and biological properties. It directly controls pore-size distribution, and through it water retention, water movement and air movement. Well-aggregated soil holds a mix of pore sizes: micropores retain and store water, while mesopores and larger pores let water and air move in. Such soil usually takes in water faster and is not prone to ponding. In compacted soil with few aggregates and little pore space, roots grow poorly and can be cut off from stored water and nutrients. Clay, adsorbed calcium and magnesium, and {{ref:soil-chem-163}} act as cementing agents, while exchangeable sodium lowers stability by promoting dispersion. Tillage, machinery traffic and livestock traffic are the main disruptors. Reduced or zero tillage, cover crops, perennial crops and organic inputs improve aggregation, whereas heavy or irregular rainfall, and warmer temperatures that speed decomposition and carbon loss, can lower it. See also {{ref:soil-phys-005}}.

soil-phys-086.title: The hidden damage under farm fields
soil-phys-086.text: Erosion is easy to see. Compaction mostly is not. Unlike salt build-up or erosion, compaction of farmland is mainly a hidden problem below the surface, and finding it takes special methods. Soil compaction in agriculture is the rise in bulk density, or fall in porosity, of farmland soil under loads from outside or within. It is also called soil structure degradation. It can harm nearly all the physical, chemical and biological properties and functions of soil. Together with erosion it has been called the costliest and most serious environmental problem of conventional agriculture. Heavy machinery and poor management can press the subsoil into impermeable layers that hold back the movement of water and nutrients. On the farm, compaction cuts crop growth, yield and quality. Beyond it, compaction adds runoff, erosion, emissions of gases that warm the climate ({{ref:soil-phys-246}}), nutrients fouling lakes and rivers, less water reaching the groundwater, and loss of biodiversity. The problem is old. Hard layers below the plough, described in {{ref:soil-agri-101}}, were linked to compaction before farming was mechanized, and modern techniques have raised the risk. In 1991 compaction was estimated at 4% of human-caused damage to soils worldwide, some 68.3 million hectares. In 2013 it was a major cause of damage in Europe (about 33 million ha), Africa (18 million ha), Asia (10 million ha) and Australia (4 million ha). In Europe about 32% of subsoils are highly vulnerable to it and 18% moderately so.

soil-phys-095.title: How water climbs above the groundwater
soil-phys-095.text: Water in soil does not stop at the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. It climbs into the small pores above, held there by {{ref:soil-phys-260}} under negative pressure. This is {{ref:soil-phys-252}} in soil. For some distance above that level the soil can be fully saturated; higher up it is still wet, but holds less water with every step of height. Pore size sets the climb, from about a centimetre in coarse sand to tens of metres in silt or clay. Water held at negative pressure pulls particles together, so effective stress can stay positive even at a free surface. That is why a wet sand castle stands, held by friction where grains touch, and collapses once it is submerged. Negative pore pressures are much stronger in clay than in sand. They explain why clay soils shrink as they dry and swell when wetted, which can damage light structures and roads.

soil-phys-130.title: Moisture stress and the root's chemical alarm
soil-phys-130.text: When roots sense dry soil, they make the hormone ABA. It closes the stomata, cutting transpiration and {{ref:soil-hist-147}}, and loosens root cell walls so roots can grow in search of water. Moisture stress is the strain a plant suffers when water in its tissues falls below optimal levels, because transpiration outpaces uptake by the roots. Mildly stressed plants recover in 1–2 days; severely stressed ones regain only 40-60% of maximum of it the day after rewatering. Well-timed irrigation avoids it by replacing soil water before stress sets in. In strongly acidic soils, aluminum toxicity can cause it even when the soil is fairly moist.

soil-phys-159.title: Needle ice: frost columns that heave seedlings from the ground
soil-phys-159.text: On a cold night, columns of ice can grow straight up out of bare soil. Needle ice is needle-shaped columns of ice that grow from groundwater at the soil surface. It forms when the soil is above 0 °C but the air at the surface is below 0 °C: water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column. Needles are typically a few centimeters long. Ten centimeters is the recorded maximum, though specimens of 15-20 cm have been seen at Gerðuberg. It needs {{ref:soil-phys-179}}, in which supercooled water freezes onto existing ice in a porous medium, and it favors soils high in silt and organic matter. It is {{ref:soil-phys-153}} at the start of the freezing season, before there is any soil overburden to lift. Taber found that pore size controls the amount of frost heave, and that a gradient of soil moisture tension drives water up toward the freezing front near the surface. Growing needles lift soil particles and crusts, which settle unevenly on melting. They disturb streambanks, aid soil creep and shape {{ref:soil-phys-163}}. They also heave seedlings out of the ground, and the seedlings often die because they do not resettle or their roots dry out. Swedish pipkrake, coined in 1907 by Henrik Hesselman, is one of several names. Others are frost pillars, Kammeis and shimobashira. See {{ref:soil-phys-137}} for the soil temperatures involved.

soil-phys-174.title: Tortuosity: the long way through the pores
soil-phys-174.text: A straight line scores exactly 1. The simplest measure of tortuosity is that arc-chord ratio: a path's actual length divided by the straight-line distance between its ends. Winding pore channels score higher. The concept has many definitions. Hydraulic, electrical, spreading-related and thermal tortuosities describe different transport processes, while geometrical tortuosity describes pore shape. In the study of underground water it is the ratio of diffusivity in free space to diffusivity in the porous medium. Strictly, effective diffusivity varies with the inverse square of geometrical tortuosity. In soils, flow-path tortuosity controls how solutes spread ({{ref:soil-phys-240}}) during leaching, and the tortuosity of large pores indicates their resistance to water flow.

soil-phys-195.title: Molecular diffusion, fast over millimeters, slow over meters
soil-phys-195.text: Double the distance and diffusion takes four times as long. The random thermal movement of molecules ({{ref:soil-phys-243}}) carries solutes from high to low concentration in the {{ref:soil-found-079}}. Over small distances it matters, but it spreads solutes slowly over large ones. Its coefficient is small and often negligible, except where groundwater barely moves, as in clay aquitards. Diffusion is a real physical process. Dispersion is an empirical factor that merely shares its mathematical form.

soil-phys-196.title: Retardation: why contaminants lag behind the water
soil-phys-196.text: A contaminant does not always travel at the speed of the water that carries it. Retardation by {{ref:soil-chem-145}} is the slowing of a contaminant's average movement relative to groundwater because it adsorbs to the soil, measured by a retardation factor. This holds the contaminant back until the amount set by the adsorption equilibrium has been adsorbed. The factor depends on the chemistry of both the contaminant and the aquifer, and it is analogous to the retardation factor of chromatography. Less soluble contaminants can move hundreds or thousands of times slower than water, so only the more soluble species travel far. This differs from the spreading described in {{ref:soil-phys-192}} and {{ref:soil-phys-193}}. Unlike diffusion and dispersion, which merely spread a contaminant, retardation changes its global average velocity, so it can be much slower than the water. Chromatography gives the clearest definition. There the retardation factor R is the fraction of the substance in the mobile phase at equilibrium: the quantity in the mobile phase divided by the total quantity in the system. In planar chromatography, RF is the substance's travel distance over the solvent front's. It always lies between 0 and 1, because nothing outruns the solvent. A spot that travels 2.5 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm gives 0.50.

soil-phys-209.title: The groundwater flow equation: diffusion underground
soil-phys-209.text: Mathematicians know it as the {{ref:soil-phys-241}}. The groundwater flow equation describes how groundwater moves through a porous medium. It is usually derived by combining Darcy's law with conservation of mass in a small control volume. The compressibility of both fluid and matrix enters it: clay's is 10−6 to 10−8 Pa−1, against 10−7 to 10−9 for sand. Its solutions do practical work. The Theis and Thiem equations, its transient and steady-state solutions for flow to a well, are used in pumping tests. The Hooghoudt equation applies it to drainage by pipes, tile drains or ditches.

soil-phys-215.title: Penman–Monteith: estimating evaporation from the weather
soil-phys-215.text: Evapotranspiration can be estimated without measuring it directly. The Penman–Monteith equation does it from meteorological data. Penman published it in 1948 and Monteith revised it in 1965. Its inputs include net irradiance, ground heat flux, vapor pressure deficit, air density and {{ref:soil-phys-242}}, and atmospheric and stomatal conductance. Stomatal conductance captures leaf area index, water stress and CO2, so the result is sensitive to vegetation. The FAO recommends the equation, though errors against direct measurement can range from -9 to 40%. In 1998 the FAO simplified it as FAO 56, which computes {{ref:soil-phys-217}} in mm per day from radiation, temperature, wind at 2 m and vapor pressure deficit. Stress coefficients cut the estimate for waterlogged soil starving roots of oxygen, dry soil causing wilt, and salinity. GIS-linked hydrologic models such as SWAT use it.

soil-phys-229.title: Three kinds of compaction and how to tell them apart
soil-phys-229.text: Each kind of compaction has different signs and different remedies, so diagnosis comes first. Surface seals show broken-down aggregates, poor seedling emergence and fast runoff and erosion. Sandy loams and silt loams are especially prone, because their unstable aggregates leave small particles that fill pores into dense crusts. Surface layer compaction shows as deep wheel tracks, standing water, cloddy tillage and stubby, crooked roots with few root hairs. A penetrometer, wire flag or shovel dig can confirm it. Freshly plowed soil can falsely look uncompacted because it is loose at first, while no-tilled soil is firmer but has strong structure and worm-made large pores. Compaction of the subsoil ({{ref:soil-env-320}}) is found with a penetrometer in field-moist soil, which often meets much higher resistance at the base of the plow layer (typically 6 to 8 inches), and by roots that are absent below the pan or run sideways above it. Compacted soil that stays wet becomes anaerobic, causing stunted growth and {{ref:soil-fert-108}} losses shown by yellow leaves. Weakened crops are more prone to root diseases such as Pythium and Fusarium. For background, see {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-236.title: Managing field traffic to spare the soil
soil-phys-236.text: Most compaction is avoidable if the right passes are changed. Judge traffic by soil moisture at the time and by equipment weight and load distribution. Late dry planting does little damage, but wet-harvest trucks and spring plowing of wet clay loam do much. Tracks greatly reduce {{ref:soil-env-320}}. Multiple axles, and wide tires at low inflation pressure, spread loads, and most compaction comes from the first tire passing. Dual wheels enlarge the footprint but cut it less, because pressure cones merge at shallow depth, and they tempt fieldwork on wet soil. Poorly drained fields suffer worse compaction; {{ref:soil-phys-227}} dries the subsoil, and surface shaping and mole drains suit heavy clay. The problem itself is in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}.

soil-phys-238.title: Critical state: when soil flows like a frictional fluid
soil-phys-238.text: The branch of soil mechanics called {{ref:soil-phys-105}} models saturated remoulded soils on the critical state concept. At the critical state, stress and strain relate constantly: the soil keeps deforming without any further rise in stress, like a frictional fluid. In practice this marks failure. The concept was published in 1958 by Roscoe, Schofield and Wroth, from Cambridge simple shear tests and Imperial College triaxial tests. The Cam-Clay models assume an isotropic, elasto-plastic soil with no creep, and the Modified Cam-Clay of John Burland uses an elliptical yield surface. It extends the ideas of {{ref:soil-phys-101}} and {{ref:soil-phys-073}}.

soil-phys-258.title: Osmosis: why salty soil starves roots of water
soil-phys-258.text: Salty soil can leave a plant short of water even when the ground is wet. Osmosis explains why. It is the net movement of solvent through a selectively permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration, which is the same as from high to low {{ref:soil-water-172}}. The pressure needed from outside to stop that net flow is the {{ref:soil-chem-216}}. It is a colligative property, so it depends on the solute's molar concentration and not on its identity. Osmotic transport is a pressure-driven viscous flow of solvent, not the random spreading of molecules. In a plant cell, osmotic entry of water raises turgor pressure until it equals it. In a hypertonic solution water leaves and the cell shrinks; in a hypotonic one it swells turgid. Roots take in water and nutrients across cell membranes by osmosis, so excess salt in the soil lowers water uptake and can cause leaf burn.

soil-water-003.title: How rain and runoff carry soil away
soil-water-003.text: Almost 36 billion tons of soil are lost to water every year, according to a global model. Water erosion is the removal of soil by rainfall and by the surface runoff it produces, a form of {{ref:soil-water-001}}. It begins with the rain itself. Raindrops bombard aggregates and detach small particles that are easily transported, by splash or by water running downhill, to a low area where they are deposited. Runoff, the flow described in {{ref:soil-water-019}}, begins when the soil is saturated or when rain falls faster than water can infiltrate (see {{ref:soil-water-180}}). Runoff with enough flow energy carries loosened soil particles down the slope as sediment. Rain and runoff cause four main types of erosion, in rising severity: splash, sheet, {{ref:soil-water-025}} and {{ref:soil-water-027}}. Concentrated runoff cuts small channels called rills. If runoff keeps deepening them, they may grow into gullies, a gully being a rill too deep for tillage equipment to smooth. Sheet erosion ({{ref:soil-water-005}}) and rilling cause most soil erosion. The damage is not evenly spread, either. Water erosion removes soil mainly from the middle and lower parts of a slope rather than from hilltops.

soil-water-105.title: Soil loss tolerance: how much erosion is too much
soil-water-105.text: How fast can a soil lose its top layer and still farm well forever? Soil loss tolerance, the T value, answers in tons per acre per year: the maximum average yearly loss that still lets a soil sustain current production economically and indefinitely. T values range from 1 to 5. Devised by the US agency for {{ref:soil-agri-059}}, the idea rests on the minimum rate of loss that would deplete organic matter and harm crop productivity. It is calculated with the formula T=υQρC+R(1−C). In 1961-1962 US soil groups were given T values of 2 to 6, later adjusted to 1 to 5, and conservation management adopted it from the mid-1960s. In depth terms, a soil deeper than 5 feet has a T of 5 tons per acre per year (11 metric tons per hectare), about 0.03 inch of depth a year, or 1 inch in 33 years. T is lower for shallow soils: with rooting depth under 10 inches it equals 0.006 inch a year, or 1 inch in 167 years. By 2007, 99 million acres, 28% of US cropland, were eroding faster than T, down from 169 million acres, 40% of cropland, in 1982. The value's validity is questioned. Critics note that T values vary across space, may not hold where soluble carbonates abound, as in karst, and should be weighed against actual soil loss. {{ref:soil-water-001}} is the loss it measures.

soil-water-156.title: Saturated and unsaturated flow: pushed by gravity, pulled by suction
soil-water-156.text: Water in soil moves in two quite different ways, and the line between them sits at field capacity ({{ref:soil-water-177}}). Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to field capacity, gravity and differences in water pressure push water away from where it was applied. That is saturated flow. At higher suctions the push gives way to a pull. Water's {{ref:soil-phys-253}} to soil solids sets up a suction gradient, which draws water from wetter to drier soil and from macropores to micropores. That is unsaturated flow. The lab manual states the same split in other units: saturated flow at tensions of 0 to -0.3 bar, driven by hydrostatic head, and unsaturated flow at 0.3 to 31 bars, driven by a tension gradient. ({{ref:soil-water-172}} explains these suctions.) Unsaturated flow is slow, at most about 2.5 cm a day, so roots keep dying back and growing toward moister soil. It slows because the connected wet pathways shrink as soil dries. {{ref:soil-water-193}} therefore depends on water content, and it falls in a very non-linear way as soil dries. Six factors control infiltration and movement: texture, structure, organic matter, depth to impervious layers such as hardpans or bedrock, water already present, and {{ref:soil-phys-137}}. Warm soils take in water faster, while frozen soils such as permafrost may not absorb it at all, depending on how they froze. {{ref:soil-water-238}} gives the rate of change of moisture in unsaturated soil. Lewis Richardson first published it in 1922, and software such as Hydrus solves it numerically.

soil-water-172.title: Water potential: why water flows from soil to sky
soil-water-172.text: Water climbs from soil into roots, up a stem, out through the leaves and into the air without any pump. Each step has a more negative water potential than the one before, so the water flows passively. Water potential is the potential energy of water per unit volume, compared with pure water under reference conditions. In soils the reference is usually pure water at the soil surface. Written with the Greek letter ψ, it expresses water's tendency to move because of {{ref:soil-phys-258}}, gravity, mechanical pressure and matrix effects such as capillary action. Unrestricted water moves from higher to lower potential. Dissolved solutes lower the potential; added pressure raises it. In soil, total potential sums three parts: {{ref:soil-water-173}} from capillary action, an osmotic part in saline soil and a gravitational part that drives downward flow. A saturated soil sits at 0 kPa. After free drainage, at {{ref:soil-water-177}}, it is −33 kPa, and at the {{ref:soil-water-178}} −1500 kPa. Dry air is typically about −100 MPa. No single instrument covers the whole range. Electrical resistance blocks read from −90 to −1500 kPa, while {{ref:soil-water-223}} reaches −10,000 kPa.

soil-water-215.title: Draining farmland, from Dutch steam pumps to Florida citrus
soil-water-215.text: In the Netherlands, 15th-century windpumps could drain only marginal land. The Haarlemmermeer had to wait for large steam pumps, which drained it between 1849 and 1852. Agricultural land drainage removes excess water from farmland, from wetland soils to fields waterlogged for short spells, so that crops are not damaged. Clay-rich soils pass water down very slowly, and hardpans or shallow rock block it. When excess water shuts out air, roots suffocate. Even excellent soils waterlogged for a week of the year can lose their fruit trees. Ditches turned glacial marshes in the northern United States and Europe into mucklands for vegetables and other high-value crops. Florida's flatwoods citrus groves are pumped after heavy rain. Rice needs complete water control, since fields are flooded or drained at different stages. Loss of water to air from soil and plants ({{ref:soil-water-161}}) concentrates the salts in irrigation water, so irrigated land may need periodic over-irrigation and drainage. {{ref:soil-chem-030}} are an exception: subsurface drainage is normally not advisable, though surface drainage in rainy periods can help reclaim them.
